question:
A sequence of squares is made of identical square tiles. The edge of each square is one tile length longer than the edge of the previous square. The first three squares are shown. How many more tiles does the seventh square require than the sixth?

[Figure 1](figures/2002_AMC_8_Q11_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
The first three squares have side lengths of 1, 2, and 3 tiles. Since each new side is one tile longer, the sixth square has 6 rows of 6 tiles, and the seventh has 7 rows of 7 tiles. Their tile counts are therefore \(6\times6=36\) and \(7\times7=49\).

Subtracting gives the number of additional tiles:
\[
49-36=13.
\]
The seventh square requires \(13\) more tiles, choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
The figure begins with a square one tile across, so the sixth square is 6 tiles across and the seventh is 7 tiles across.

Imagine keeping the sixth square in one corner of the seventh. Add a column of 6 tiles beside it, making a rectangle 6 tiles tall and 7 tiles wide. Then add a row of 7 tiles across the top. These two added pieces fill the larger square, and they do not overlap. Thus the number of new tiles is
\[
6+7=13.
\]
The answer is \(13\) more tiles, choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
solutionMethods.label: Count only the added tiles

reference.question:
A sequence of squares is made of identical square tiles. The edge of each square is one tile length longer than the edge of the previous square. The first three squares are shown. How many more tiles does the seventh square require than the sixth?

[Figure 1](figures/2002_AMC_8_Q11_question_fig1.svg)
reference.solution:
Method 1: Count rows of tiles

The first three squares have side lengths of 1, 2, and 3 tiles. Since each new side is one tile longer, the sixth square has 6 rows of 6 tiles, and the seventh has 7 rows of 7 tiles. Their tile counts are therefore \(6\times6=36\) and \(7\times7=49\).

Subtracting gives the number of additional tiles:
\[
49-36=13.
\]
The seventh square requires \(13\) more tiles, choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

Method 2: Count only the added tiles

The figure begins with a square one tile across, so the sixth square is 6 tiles across and the seventh is 7 tiles across.

Imagine keeping the sixth square in one corner of the seventh. Add a column of 6 tiles beside it, making a rectangle 6 tiles tall and 7 tiles wide. Then add a row of 7 tiles across the top. These two added pieces fill the larger square, and they do not overlap. Thus the number of new tiles is
\[
6+7=13.
\]
The answer is \(13\) more tiles, choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

nodes.description: Generate a number or shape pattern that follows a given rule. Identify apparent features of the pattern that were not explicit in the rule itself. For example, given the rule “Add 3” and the starting number 1, generate terms in the resulting sequence and observe that the terms appear to alternate between odd and even numbers. Explain informally why the numbers will continue to alternate in this way.
nodes.label: 4.OA.C.5

nodes.description: Identify arithmetic patterns (including patterns in the addition table or multiplication table), and explain them using properties of operations . For example, observe that 4 times a number is always even, and explain why 4 times a number can be decomposed into two equal addends.
nodes.label: 3.OA.D.9

nodes.description: Apply properties of operations as strategies to multiply and divide.* Examples: If 6 × 4 = 24 is known, then 4 × 6 = 24 is also known. (Commutative property of multiplication.) 3 × 5 × 2 can be found by 3 × 5 = 15, then 15 × 2 = 30, or by 5 × 2 = 10, then 3 × 10 = 30. (Associative property of multiplication.) Knowing that 8 × 5 = 40 and 8 × 2 = 16, one can find 8 × 7 as 8 × (5 + 2) = (8 × 5) + (8 × 2) = 40 + 16 = 56. (Distributive property.) *Students need not use formal terms for these properties.
nodes.label: 3.OA.B.5

nodes.description: Determine whether a group of objects (up to 20) has an odd or even number of members, e.g., by pairing objects or counting them by 2s; write an equation to express an even number as a sum of two equal addends.

edges.scope: The take-away meaning of subtraction in the explicit total-minus-part relation

edges.reason: Two-digit notation broadens the sequences that can be continued. The source gives no required up-to-100 range, so Gemini imports a standard exercise format into the criterion; smaller examples establish constant additive change directly.
The constant-increase cases include small additive steps whose values are within-ten addition facts; this is the addition component of the pattern procedure.
The rectangle/square area formulas count equal square units, so the meaning of area and its uniform unit are part of the asserted result.
edges.scope: interpreting length times width as unit-square count

edges.reason: The prerequisite specifically continues a constant additive change. Dot patterns can instead grow by changing increments, such as consecutive square arrays, and be continued geometrically. Both external necessity judgments conflate general additive increments with the narrower constant-change scope.
edges.scope: Constant-additive-change examples before general graphical number patterns
